A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and provide readable text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. Existing experiments, prompts, and transcripts can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original COVID-19 human experiments, COVID-19 and climate LLM-judge experiments, and calibration and persuasion analyses in Sections 2–3 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those original results and adds a human climate-change experiment and an education-stratified analysis of COVID-19 sessions.

M1.justification: The proposed three-round debate procedure, source-supported arguments, and naive and persona-conditioned LLM judges remain unchanged. Appendix E retains the substantive prompt templates. Newly documented source balancing does not establish a change to the underlying method.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates climate claims only with LLM judges. V2 extends human evaluation to Climate-Fever claims with 146 participants selected for contrasting climate beliefs. This substantially expands the human study's domain and population coverage; climate data themselves were already represented in v1.

E2.justification: V2 evaluates a preferred-position consultancy variant in the new human climate study: consultants choose their answer and are correct 92.5% of the time. This extends the baseline beyond assigned-position consultancy. The original COVID-19 comparator and the GPT-4o, Qwen, and zero-shot comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The added human climate evaluation introduces 73 participants per belief group, 421 debate sessions, and 424 consultancy sessions, with consultants selecting their positions. This is an additional evaluation design, not a revision of the retained COVID-19 experiment, which still uses three rounds, GPT-4o at temperature 0.2, and 448 sessions per protocol.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds an analysis of educational attainment and belief-switching rates across the existing 896 COVID-19 sessions. The earlier calibration, belief-interaction, model-strength, speaking-order, and persuasion-strategy analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions use standard-error bars, significance tests, and confidence intervals for the existing analyses. The new climate results extend the same reporting practice; no new repeated-run counts, seeds, or uncertainty-estimation procedures are documented.

E6.justification: V2 adds human climate accuracy results of 72.1% for debate versus 68.3% for preferred-position consultancy in Section 2.2 and Figure 1. Appendix D.1 adds education-specific belief-switching results, including 15.9% versus 36.2% for PhD holders. These are additional findings; matched COVID-19 and LLM results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The mixed-effects logistic-regression equations and definitions of accuracy and belief updates are retained. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations that change between versions.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the human-effectiveness claim from COVID-19 to climate change, including superiority over preferred-position consultancy. The central debate and persona-judge contributions remain. The conclusion narrows its deployment characterization from a practical, scalable mechanism for high-stakes domains to a promising approach for belief-sensitive factual assessment.

C2.justification: V2 adds deployment use cases, targeted-manipulation risks, and requirements for verifiable ground truth and domain-specific validation. Appendix A proposes longitudinal prediction-market studies to distinguish mainstream bias from truth seeking. Appendix D.1 newly interprets reduced education-specific belief switching as protection against manipulation.

D1.justification: Section 2.1.2 newly discloses equal source counts for opposing positions and selection of credible-appearing misinformation sources. Appendix A adds deployment-resource guidance, while Appendix C.3 removes the exact recruitment-cost breakdown. The code/data URL and substantive prompt templates are retained; actual resource availability changes are not established.

R1.justification: The introduction newly positions debate against single-advisor misinformation interventions, citing Costello and colleagues [15, 16], previously used for persuasion analysis. The related-work discussion and cited-work set otherwise remain substantially unchanged; reference [53] receives a publication and metadata update.

P1.justification: V2 revises the abstract and introduction, separates several results into clearer paragraph headings, and adds an Ethical Statement and NeurIPS checklist. These are localized editorial and structural changes; the main section organization and extensive prompt and transcript appendices remain largely intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned to display COVID-19 and climate results together. The workflow diagram is revised and moved from appendix Figure 6 to main-text Figure 2. Several captions clarify COVID-19 scope, and displays shift with text reflow; the remaining figures and tables are substantially retained.

improvement.justification: The new human climate experiment strengthens generalization evidence and tests debate against consultants choosing their own answers. Source-selection disclosures and specific deployment limitations also help. These gains are tempered by inconsistent consultancy descriptions in Figure 2 and an education analysis that infers improved judgment from belief-switching rates without establishing whether those switches correct errors.
